 The best laptop power banks are a must-buy when you're working away from a power socket. After all, even the best laptops for photo editing won't run on battery forever. And with governments telling us all to stock up on food and prepare for power outages, a power bank is a great way of ensuring you can keep vital devices going for a few days if the mains electricity fails to flow.
 But, the best iPhone power banks won't be powerful enough to do the job. Instead, you'll need a power bank with at least 18,000mAh capacity, as well as the right ports to connect to your specific laptop.
 As an added bonus, with a power bank this powerful, you'll be able to charge your cameras, tablets, phones,and other devices too. To find you the best model for your needs, we've put our experts to work. They've been testing and reviewing power banks, as well as using them within their own workflows, in order to compile this list of the absolute best.

 The DJI Power 1000 is a rugged, high-capacity power station designed with drone users in mind. With 1,024Wh of capacity and 2,200W continuous output (4,400W peak), it provides ample power for charging multiple drone batteries, cameras, and other essential gear on location. The two USB-C ports (140W each) allow for fast charging, while the SDC and SDC Lite ports support DJI’s proprietary adapters for even more efficient drone charging.
 Weighing 13kg, the Power 1000 is not the lightest option, but its sturdy build and rounded handles make it easy to carry. The clear display offers essential battery information, though it lacks smart features like an app or battery health monitoring. Additionally, there’s no built-in light or wireless charging, which could be a drawback for some users.
 Despite these limitations, the DJI Power 1000 excels at providing reliable, high-wattage power for drone operators and creatives working off-grid. Whether you're filming in remote locations or need a dependable backup power source, this station delivers efficient, high-speed charging for DJI drones and other kit.

 This power bank stands out for two main reasons. One is its impressive 48,000mAh capacity, which makes it capable of charging an iPhone 15 Pro nearly 11 times. The second is its ability to charge up to five devices at the same time, with a maximum output of 300W. That makes it particularly well-suited for camping trips, weekend hikes, or emergency power situations.
 Despite its somewhat hefty weight of 1.86 kg, the power bank features a sleek design with high-quality materials, including a low-light display that provides real-time information about battery level and power input/output. Equipped with two USB-A ports and three USB-C ports, the power bank offers versatile charging options.
 It's likely to last you a while too; Ugreen claims the device will retain 80% of its capacity after 3,000 charge cycles. However, our reviewer also noted a few drawbacks, such as its heavy weight, the lack of an included charging plug, and variable charging speeds depending on the cables used.

With enough capacity to charge your phone several times over, or run your camera and accessories off while on long shoots away from a constant power supply.
 However it isn't the only 25,000mAh capacity power bank on the market, so if you don't need its fast charging powers then you can get cheaper and lighter options elsewhere (or from UGREEN themselves), and the complex and varying power outputs might just be enough to put a lot of people off.

 You don't really need to have an informative screen on your power bank, but the Anker Prime power bank has the easiest power percentage and countdown timer for charging/discharging the battery I have used yet. And knowing exactly how fast my laptop is charging is both just plain interesting to know, but I can also plan ahead to give make sure I have enough juice left throughout the day.
 The Anker Prime power isn’t just about a screen though, it also has a solid 20,000mAh of battery which I managed to get a few days' worth of keeping my phone and laptop going with short bursts of recharging, or one big recharge of my MacBook Pro 13. The big 200W maximum output, with a 100W single port output, also allowed me to use my laptop at full power. The power bank is a little boxy for slipping into pockets, but it looks great.
 Read more: Anker Prime 20,000mAh Power Bank (200W) review 
 FAQs 
 Will one of the best portable chargers work for a laptop?
 Sadly not, you will need a power bank with a much higher capacity than most power banks used to charge camera phones or other small appliances. It's recommended that you invest in a power bank with a 20,000 mAh or larger especially if you want to charge it multiple times. 
 How do I connect my laptop to the powerbank?
 How you connect your laptop to your power bank will depend on the time of charging cable your laptop needs. While most modern laptops such as the Apple Macbook Pro 14 M2 will have a USB C input, some older models might still use round AC adapters or a standard USB A input. You will be able to get the correct cable from Amazon.

 Is 100W enough for a MacBook Pro?

 Yes, but results depend on how the charger splits power between ports. The best models keep the main USB-C port strong enough for laptop charging while still leaving useful output for a second device.

 For long-haul journeys, I recommend wired car chargers instead because they support much faster charging speeds and let you recharge several devices at once. If you're traveling with a laptop or a Chromebook, your car charger needs to support at least 60W to 65W minimum to be compatible.
 That's not enough power to be split between two devices, though, which is where the best 100W car chargers come in. I have used countless car chargers through the years.  How to Choose the Best USB-C Car Charger for Your Laptop
 Choosing the right USB-C car charger for your laptop comes down to four factors: wattage, ports, build quality, and vehicle compatibility. Get any of these wrong and you will end up with a charger that either does not work, runs too hot, or pops your cigarette lighter fuse. Here is what our team learned over three months of testing.
 Match Wattage to Your Laptop’s Needs
 The first rule is simple: your charger must deliver at least the wattage your laptop draws under load. A MacBook Air M2 only needs 45W, so a 65W charger is enough. A MacBook Pro 16 M3 Max needs 140W for fast charging, so anything below 100W will charge slowly or not at all. Check your laptop’s power adapter: it will say something like “20V/3.25A (65W)” on the label. Buy a car charger that can deliver at least that wattage, and ideally 25-50 percent more for headroom.
 Understand PD vs QC Protocols
 USB-C Power Delivery (PD) is the protocol that negotiates high-wattage charging between your laptop and the charger. Quick Charge (QC) is a Qualcomm protocol primarily for phones. For laptop charging, you need PD, specifically PD 3.0 for up to 100W or PD 3.1 for up to 240W. A charger that only supports QC will fast-charge your phone but trickle-charge your laptop or not charge it at all. Every charger on our list supports PD 3.0 or higher.
 Vehicle Fuse Compatibility and Safety
 Most 12V cigarette lighter outlets are fused at 10A-15A, which means they can deliver 120W-180W before tripping. A 200W+ charger will technically work, but it may pop your fuse under sustained load. The UGREEN, Anker, LISEN, and other premium chargers on our list include protection circuits that prevent fuse trips by throttling output when they detect a weak electrical connection. Cheap chargers often skip this protection, which can damage your vehicle’s electrical system.
 Multi-Port Chargers and Power Allocation
 Multi-port chargers split their total wattage across ports dynamically. A 200W charger with three ports does not deliver 200W to each port; it delivers up to 100W to one port, less to the others, depending on demand. If you need to charge two laptops at full speed, you need a charger with two high-wattage USB-C ports like the NXPGKEA above. For laptop + phone + tablet, a standard multi-port charger works fine.

The LISEN 200W GaN on our list is the standout example: it stays noticeably cooler under sustained load than silicon-based competitors. If you live in a hot climate or charge your laptop at high wattage frequently, GaN is worth the premium.

 A 3-foot cable works for front-seat use but falls short for back-seat passengers. If you regularly have passengers in the back seat, look for chargers with 6-foot+ cables like the PWR+ above. Also, make sure your cable is rated for the wattage you need. A 3A cable caps out at 60W; for 100W+ charging, you need a 5A e-marked cable. The Anker, NXPGKEA, and LISEN above all include high-quality cables.
 UL Certification and Build Quality

The PWR+ on our list is UL Listed, and the UGREEN, Anker, and LISEN have equivalent safety certifications from other agencies. Avoid no-name chargers that lack safety certification; the savings are not worth the risk to your laptop or vehicle.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a USB-C car charger actually charge a laptop?
 Yes. A USB-C car charger with Power Delivery (PD) support can charge a laptop, provided it delivers enough wattage. Most modern laptops need 45W-100W; high-performance models like the 16-inch MacBook Pro need up to 140W. Look for chargers that explicitly list PD 3.0 or PD 3.1 support and a wattage rating that meets or exceeds your laptop’s power adapter output. Standard phone chargers under 45W cannot charge a laptop under load.
 What wattage USB-C car charger do I need for my laptop?
 Match the wattage to your laptop’s original charger. A MacBook Air needs 45W, a MacBook Pro 13 needs 60W-67W, a MacBook Pro 14 needs 70W-96W, a MacBook Pro 16 needs 140W for fast charging, a Dell XPS 13 needs 45W, a Dell XPS 15 needs 130W, an HP Spectre x360 needs 65W-90W, and a Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon needs 45W-65W. Add 25 percent headroom for charging under heavy workload.
 What is the difference between USB-C PD and Quick Charge?
 USB-C Power Delivery (PD) is the universal standard for high-wattage USB-C charging up to 240W, used by laptops, tablets, and modern phones. Quick Charge (QC) is a Qualcomm proprietary standard primarily used by Android phones, capping out around 18W-36W. For laptop charging, you need PD. A QC-only charger will charge your phone fast but will either trickle-charge or fail to charge your laptop. Most modern multi-port chargers support both PD and QC for device compatibility.
 Is it safe to charge a laptop with a car charger?
 Yes, as long as the charger is from a reputable brand, supports USB-C PD, and has safety certifications like UL Listed or equivalent. Premium chargers include protection against over-voltage, over-current, short-circuit, and over-temperature events. Avoid no-name chargers that lack safety certification: they can damage your laptop battery or your vehicle’s electrical system. Stick with brands like Anker, UGREEN, LISEN, Satechi, and Baseus that have established track records.
 Can a USB-C car charger drain my car battery?
 A USB-C car charger only draws power when the vehicle is on (or in accessory mode). When the engine is off, most modern cars cut power to the 12V cigarette outlet, so there is no drain. If your vehicle powers the 12V outlet continuously, leaving a charger plugged in draws a small parasitic load (under 0.5W) that will not drain a healthy battery in a day or two. For long-term parking, unplug the charger to be safe.
 Final Verdict: Which USB-C Car Charger Should You Buy?

If you are a daily commuter with a single laptop and want the safest all-around pick, the UGREEN 130W is our editor’s choice: nearly 6,000 reviewers back it, and our testing confirms the wattage claims. If you are a MacBook Pro power user who needs 100W from a single port and values Anker’s reliability, the Anker 167.5W Max is the smart buy. If you run a mobile office or travel with family, the LISEN 200W GaN or CHIPOFY 300W cover every device without breaking a sweat.
 Budget shoppers should look at the Yenyoh 100W for a no-frills single-port charger or the YURCIPWE 100W if you want a USB-A port for your phone. Back-seat laptop users will love the PWR+ 90W with its 10-foot cord. And if you need to charge two laptops at full 100W simultaneously, the NXPGKEA 200W is the only charger on our list that delivers.
 Whatever you choose, make sure it supports USB-C PD 3.0 or higher, matches or exceeds your laptop’s wattage requirement, and comes from a brand with safety certifications.  The best 100W USB-C charger for most people is a compact four-port GaN model with a clear power-sharing chart; choose a two-port charger for simpler laptop-and-phone travel, or a larger desk model if you regularly charge several devices at once. The key is not the headline 100W figure alone: it is how much power remains available to the laptop when other ports are in use, and whether the charger includes a cable rated for that load.
 Quick picks by situation
 For a travel bag: Anker Prime 100W GaN Wall Charger. Its three USB-C ports and compact design suit a laptop, phone, and accessory without taking up much room.
 For a simple laptop-and-phone setup: UGREEN Nexode 100W USB-C Charger. Its four-port layout gives flexibility, though simultaneous charging reduces the power available to each device.
 For a desk with several devices: Baseus 100W GaN chargers with multiple USB-C and USB-A outputs. Check the specific model’s power-sharing chart: Baseus sells several chargers with different layouts and allocations.
 For a charger-and-cable bundle: Choose a model explicitly sold with a 5A, 100W-capable USB-C cable. Bundles vary by retailer and product version, so verify the box contents before buying.
 Comparison: ports, power sharing, and travel size

 How to choose for your actual charging routine
 For a laptop and phone on the move
 A two- or three-port charger is usually the easier travel choice. Fewer ports mean less temptation to expect full laptop speed while several devices are connected. Look for a single USB-C output that reaches 100W, plus a published two-device allocation such as 65W for the laptop and 30W for the phone. That pairing is ample for many ultrabooks and phones, although some larger laptops charge faster at higher wattages.
 Compactness is more than the charger’s dimensions. A foldable plug, a shape that does not block neighboring outlets, and a cable short enough to manage in a hotel room can make a larger difference than shaving a few grams off the adapter.
 For a desk with several devices
 Choose by the simultaneous-use chart, not by counting ports. A four-port charger may offer less laptop power than a two-port model when three devices are plugged in. If your laptop needs 65W and you also want to charge a tablet and phone, confirm that the chosen combination preserves at least 65W for the laptop. USB-A ports are handy for older accessories, but they generally do not provide the same modern USB-C Power Delivery options.
 For a laptop that draws close to 100W
 Check the laptop’s original adapter rating and whether it accepts 100W USB-C Power Delivery. Some gaming and workstation laptops require a proprietary adapter, draw more than 100W under heavy load, or charge slowly through USB-C. A 100W charger can still be useful for light work or travel, but it may not replace the original power supply in every situation.
 The cable can limit the charger
 A 100W-capable charger does not guarantee 100W charging through any USB-C cable. For power above 60W, use a cable rated for 5A and 100W or higher, typically with an e-marker chip. A cable included in the box is convenient only if its rating is stated. If the listing does not specify the cable’s wattage, budget for a known 100W-or-higher USB-C cable rather than assuming an ordinary charging cable will work.
 For a simple power check, compare the charger’s output with the laptop’s requirement. If a laptop is rated for 65W and the charger assigns it 65W when a phone is connected, the arrangement meets the adapter’s rated input target. If the charger instead drops that port to 45W, the laptop may charge more slowly, particularly during demanding work. This is why the power-sharing table matters more than the total printed on the charger.
 Ownership details that affect everyday use
 Heat is normal, but airflow matters. Small GaN chargers can become warm at high output. Avoid covering the adapter or leaving it pressed against bedding or a bag while in use.
 Expect renegotiation when plugging in devices. Adding or removing a device can briefly interrupt charging as the charger reallocates power. This is normal for many multiport designs.
 Protect the ports and cable ends. Dust and strain are common causes of charging trouble. Unplug by holding the connector, not pulling the cable, and keep the adapter dry.
 Travel compatibility still matters. Check the charger’s input-voltage range and plug design for your destination. A plug adapter may be needed; it does not convert voltage.
 Bottom line
 For a compact travel setup, the Anker Prime 100W is a strong fit if its port allocation matches your laptop-and-phone combination. For more connection options, consider a UGREEN Nexode or a specific Baseus 100W model, then compare its exact sharing chart and package contents. Before buying any of the best 100W USB-C chargers, confirm three things: your laptop accepts USB-C charging, the charger supplies enough power with your intended ports occupied, and the cable supports the wattage you need.
